newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Another S.Korean company defaults but banks step in.
newsitem.headline: Another S.Korean company defaults but banks step in.

text.p: Another South Korean company has failed to pay its debts, but Jinro Ltd will stay in business under an agreement between major banks to keep struggling firms afloat, its main creditor said on Tuesday.

Commercial Bank of Korea said it would not freeze bank accounts of Jinro Ltd -- the third high-profile company to default on its debts this year -- even though the company missed payment deadlines on Monday to non-bank financial instutitions.
Usually defaults on debt payments automatically lead to a suspension of all the company's bank accounts, the first step towards bankruptcy.
Jinro is South Korea's leading manufacturer of distilled spirits. It is groaning under heavy debt used to fund over-ambitious expansion.
The decision by the Commercial Bank to keep Jinro's credit lines open sets up a potential battle between leading banks and non-bank financial institutions.

Commercial banks last week said they would continue to extend credit to the 51 largest business groups, even if they defaulted on debt repayments, as long as there was hope their operations could be salvaged.
The agreement stipulates that banks calling in loans without permission of a bank committee set up to oversee the agreement would face penalties.
But non-bank financial institutions were not party to that agreement.
Institutions such as merchant banks and savings trust firms argue that they stand to lose the most if troubled companies are allowed continued access to credit.
In recent months, non-bank financial institutions have been accused of contributing to the financial troubles of South Korean companies by routinely calling in notes on market rumours.
They have countered by saying they must demand payments because their loans are not backed by collateral.
The banks' agreement took effect on Monday, and Jinro was the first company to benefit.
A Commercial Bank official said on Tuesday Jinro failed to pay back 50.4 billion won ($56.4 million) worth of promissory notes and cheques that some non-bank financial institutions called in.
On Monday the bank announced it would bail out Jinro Ltd and five other affiliates of the debt-ridden Jinro Group, the 19th-ranked conglomerate.
The Jinro Group said last week it would sell off property and affiliates to raise cash to pay debts estimated at 3.2 trillion won.
South Korean financial markets have been rocked by the collapse of two steelmakers this year under crushing debts -- Hanbo Steel Co in January and Sammi Steel Co in March.

Separately on Tuesday, textile maker Chung Won Corp was unable to settle promissory notes called in on Monday and now faces a final deadline by the end of Tuesday, officials at the company and its prime creditor bank said.
A Chung Won official put the amount of notes at between 500 million and 600 million won.
Jinro's woes dragged down the stock market. The leading index closed down 7.4 points, or 1.06 percent, to 689.94 at midday.
